near_miss.lead: Light appearing at dawn after battle
near_miss.why_not: The light-root corresponds but the morning words do not; routine chronological prose, with no distinctive shared phrase.

near_miss.lead: A daughter named X in a royal marriage narrative
near_miss.why_not: Cognate daughter and naming material, but Norse passive naming and Greek name-plus-copula are ordinary independent identification formulas.
Norse sleep is the victims nightmare; wanting governs helping. Russian prohibition governs sleeping with a husband. No shared syntactic collocation.

near_miss.lead: Leaving a defeated kings corpse to beasts and birds
near_miss.why_not: Homer search found dogs and birds consuming corpses (Il. 13.831; 24.411), but the Norse animal terms and tearing verb do not establish a cognate collocation. The slab partners lack the carrion scene. Retain as a thematic resemblance only.

The Norse ember-hound bites a king; the Sanskrit partners describe breaking nets, not consuming fire. Homer search found πῦρ ἐσθίει (Il. 23.182), but no matching cognate wording. The reconstructed ger mapping of the hound and net cannot establish a phrase.
Bera and fero correspond, but their objects and situations do not. No shared legal formula in the Latin passage.
The Norse object is laws, not baths. Both Greek partners concern bathing, so the apparent shared wash-root rests on the wrong Norse lemma.

Norse refers to dividing and landing a whale; Latin to cutting and carrying ice. The carry verbs are cognate, but the cutting vocabulary is not an exact pair and the sequence is a practical necessity. The Norse testimony phrase has no Latin counterpart.

Norse moðor faðir is a maternal grandfather, not a coordinated pair. Irish G303000 says neither name nor mother nor father is known; Homer asks what name the parents called the visitor. Homer corpus search confirms the parental pair is common, but the Irish parents are not agents of naming. Ordinary ancestry identification does not establish this larger inherited formula.

near_miss.lead: Royal marriage, named daughter and wife
near_miss.why_not: The recurring cognate kin terms belong to straightforward genealogical and marriage prose. Greek narratives vary between remarriage, genealogy and supplication; the Russian address to a wife is different again. No distinctive repeated predicate or poetic qualification.

near_miss.lead: Sister, mother and wife as a kinship list
near_miss.why_not: The Norse law enumerates victims of prohibited killing, with father and daughter too. The chronicle describes relatives bringing women to magicians; the birchbark letter protests sister/wife status. Cognate nouns but different list structure and function; no stable inherited merism established.

near_miss.lead: Smiths of spells and crafting a poem
near_miss.why_not: Direct Rigveda search found atakṣad bráhma (1.62.13), dhíyaṃ ... atakṣam (1.109.1), and vácāṃsy ... takṣam (6.32.1). These confirm the craft metaphor, but neither the Norse smith term nor galdr is shown cognate with those words; the slab Slavic partner has no poetic craft. No anchored inherited wording.

Norse describes a horse stumbling and the riders skull striking stone; Latin lists possible locations for the mind, adding hands. The common body-part vocabulary has neither the same syntax nor the same meristic function.

Homer has an adjective describing sleepless nights; Norse has a sleepy drunken man walking at night. Herodotus gives the ordinary circumstance of sleeping at night. Cognate sleep/night words alone do not establish a distinctive phrase.

The Norse cup is full of mead in an erotic encounter; the Vedic vessel is full of soma in a ritual bull hymn. Fullness is cognate but the vessel and drink terms do not supply a second cognate member; commonplace literal description, without stronger ritual congruence.

Norse contrasts greater maternal affection with lesser paternal affection. The epic partners concern greeting parents or filial loyalty, and the Vedic passage has three mothers and three fathers. The expected kin terms do not preserve the same figure.

The Norse law describes breaking into a farmers house and carrying out his property; Vedic passages enumerate prosperity or livestock at home. Cognate wealth material is present but no distinctive shared predication or ordered merism.

Norse lágo ... um nóttina and Slavic въ ту нощь лежащю contain cognate lying and night vocabulary. They describe ordinary overnight lodging after different events; the construction is too predictable to defend as inherited poetic wording.

words.lemma: blómi (dative singular after i in preceding context)

cognate: Norse blómi and Latin flos continue the bloom/flower root bʰleh₃-, with different nominal formations.
drift_or_renewal: The life/age dependent is renewed: Norse aldr and Latin aeuum are not cognate. The governing predicate also differs.
shared_syntax: Flower/bloom head noun with a genitive of age/life, metaphorically identifying the prime of maturity.
context: The Norse speaker contrasts an old king with Harald in his prime; Lucretius explains that natural things have fixed periods in which to reach their mature prime. The exact genitival metaphor, not the accidentally retrieved new/flower pair, supports comparison. A direct Homer search additionally found the same youth-flower metaphor in a description of Aeneas, but its nouns are not asserted cognate. The Norse text is medieval prose: independent plant-growth metaphor or literary transmission remains a substantial alternative to inheritance, so confidence is low.
phrase: bloma aldrs ~ aeui ... florem: bloom/flower of life
